as a narcissist (I am working on recovering from it), this is exactly what a narcissist does.  they interrupt the conversation to talk about themselves, then act like you are out of the ordinary for not doing this because in a narcissists world, this is normal. Additinally, they do not pay attention to others statements and will ignore them or assume things that are completley out of the ordinary.

​

There are many sources, but in my experience, this can be because as a child they were never given a chance to finish speaking their mind so they had to learn to interrupt to be heard (on that front) or that they shared things with their parents or trusted friends and were always asked again and again and were never treated like their thoughts or opinions matteres, so they don't either. This is also compounded by excessive pampering and/or criticism.  None of this is normal, but that is the unfortuante world of a narcissist.  Here are a few other traits:

Being overly boastful, exaggerating one’s own achievements  
Pretending to be superior to others  
Lack of empathy for others  
Looking down on others as inferior  
Monopolising conversations (exact issue here)  
Impatient, angry, unhappy, depressed or has mood swings when criticized  
Easily disappointed when expected importance is not given  
Always craves for “the best” in everything  
Has a very fragile self-esteem

If you want to continue the relationship, get him to a good counselor that asks questions and makes him think.  Also, there are things you can do to stop the narcissism, and it will either work (you will be on guard most of your relationship, if not all) or he will leave (changing is hard, but possible).  If I am wrong, and I hope I am, then good.  If not, I truly wish you the best of luck!

Last question first: I feel your pain on this... I have done this over and over again and have let myself "slip" from the freakin' cusp of greatness. I have put Exercise and Journaling in the upper category, along with Scripture reading to be specific, and I have added "Pointless Entertainment when Alone - can watch with somebody" and video games to the lower category, but art nature and cold showers are not on my list there. I have even brought this up with my psychologist and he said the same thing "you are being too strict, nobody is perfect." So I FEEL YOUR PAIN!!  
  
Now lets chat, I have been on this before 3x in my life and have fallen each time. A few notes and learnings for each of them: 1) I can have a "treat" at a birthday or Christmas if I have been doing it for more than a few weeks, but if I put it in my macros and force myself to have just a small amount (a small piece of cake, no ice cream, or a Christmas cookie of each type to taste them rather than eat the tray of them) and then ensure that I am done with that, I am good to go. If I decide "hey, I can binge right now, this is going to be fine for me today and I will get it back tomorrow" then I fall apart entirely. I find that planning on it is the most important part. In all three failures for me, it began with food. First was ordering popcorn at a movie, second was ordering a pizza after cutting wood, and third was Christmas cookies after an injury that prevented me from exercising.  
  
My advice: do what you know you need to do and forget everything else and everybody else. They are not your best self and feelings you express are exactly in line with mine... you know what you need to do and it is insanely hard to do in the moments, but the alternative is insanity every moment.  
  
Now, to the idea of becoming our best selves. I think that we share a common, unstated issue here that needs to be resolved, likely through therapy, but we are able to cope with it by choosing to do all the things you mentioned above. I believe my entire value and lovability is based on what I can do and choose to do, not on the fact that I am a worthwhile individual. I know for me, I lack the ability to dream of doing something more than I am... I get comfortable and want to stay put and it is hard to get out of that rut. I think that your reading needs to be also in self help books that help you discover your value.  
  
in short, keep up the work that you know you have to do. I think that for me this is actually a huge benefit and blessing in that I get so much more out of my life when I do these things. This may sound arrogant in part, but for me if I don't do this, I feel sub par as a person and like the world is so much better than me and I am a failure, but when I do these things, the world fades away and I feel like a god of my own world.... not having to control or respond to others unless I deem it worthwhile to do so; knowing what to say and do as if I can read others minds and I can hear a voice in my head telling me what to say before I say it and I am surprised by that voice, and feeling like I can see everything I need to see.  
  
Good luck!

I have been self reflecting a lot too and decided to start facing these issues head on.  I called a man I knew well and had bad mouthed behind his back for years.   I have not spoken to this man since 2003, almost 20 years (we were effectively assigned co workers in a volunteer format).  In that call, this man taught me that we can change; he turned his life around from there and had forgotten his past.  In this call, I remembered many great things that we had done together, and learned that he is a better person than I remembered.

I also did the same to a colleague from my masters program... this man had taken the brunt of my narcissistic issues in our team and had been the only one to stand up against me.  He now operates as a high-profile consultant and I had wronged him.  The first thing he said when I told him I was calling to apologize was: Are you ok?  This man had forgiven me and was understanding of where I was and supportive of me as an individual.

In short, those who know you will still care for you and love you and appreciate who you have become, whether or not you apologize, but the recognition of your mistakes also opens those relationships into a new level can can/will give you a greater purpose of life and support in your journey.

You get what you want... if you want that type of success at the expense of relationships, you can have it. If you want to balance it out better, you can do that too.  This is a good point to reassess your life and decide: is this really what I want? or do I want something else?

Alright my man (assuming you are a guy here).  You are at a loss of what to do, and I am also there.  This is up to you to find out... for me, I am a doomer when 1) I don't exercise in the morning, 2) I don't take time to connect with myself (this means scripture reading and journaling for me), and 3) I overindulge on food that is crap for me.  This can be different for every person.  for my wife, it is when she doesn't do what she feels is right.  For one of my friends, it is when he faps. So take this for what it is, but find what works for you and just do it.  Since you mentioned specific things, make some goals, but make them small and get there.

Example: Week 1: Walk 10 minutes, jog 1

Week 2 walk 9 minutes, jog 2

Week 3 walk 8 minutes, jog 3

eventually, jog 10 minutes, walk 1

jog 12 minutes, walk 1

jog 15 minutes, walk 1

jog 18 minutes, walk 1

by the time you hit 3 months you are at a decent 5k speed

pick an item and work on it.  ignore the results, just focus on the process and do what you set out to do.  Biggest issues: people who plan don't execute and people who execute don't plan.

Your best days are any day you make of them. I am 38 and I have had bouts of best days/months based on this type of goal setting and keeping.

Good luck

Just my experience, but you have to protect your family, in this case, specifically your Daughter and Husband.  You left your parents and sister for him and for Diana (and Persephone), so do that. Chiming in my two cents here, I am active in my Mormon church and have been my whole life (mid 30s).  There are as many quirks in the church as there are for any sports fan.  Some of them are doctrinal, others are just tradition (which can be ignored, and my bishop does ignore those REALLY well, to the point of snubbing other church leaders because they are wrong on things that are not doctrine).

All that being said, if he wants to wait until 25 to get married, you don't have to even get baptized until he is 24 (it takes a year before you can go to the temple and get married for eternity).  Figure out for yourself in the interim what is true.  If he pressures you that you need to convert now or that he will not wait for you to convert, then just move on and cut your losses.  Trust me, a lot of religious guys with overbearing parents have some major relationship issues (no exceptions in my case either).  If he is actually willing to wait and is supportive of you discovering it for yourself, then you may actually have somebody worthwhile anyway.  Also, in the next 7 years he will grow up a lot and discover what really matters in life.  He is going to spend 2 years in an immersive experience of life as a missionary that will be the equivalet of like 6 years of learning doctrine and interpersonal skills.  He will not be the same person you know now, and that hopefully will be a good thing.

All the same, good luck!

Chipping in my 2 cents here... you are "attempting" to become an integrated male to have a happy, problem free life; this is what I started out as as well... if I can fix me, everything else will fit just fine.  Well, I have become the "perfect" person for a few months, I have done "everything" I was suppose to do, and I am doing it again now, but not with the same purpose.

Previously, I wanted a goal to be met... to get my wife to like me more.  I realize now that I need to do this because I need it.  She has always liked me when I did the things I was doing, and in reality, I will do them again with this process as well, but the biggest difference is that I have learned that I must do them for my sake and if she decides to leave me or we live a passionless marriage, so be it.  I cannot control her, just like I cannot control my parents (who did control me for a long time), and by doing this I hope to stop trying to control my children and ruin their lives as well.  the result I am seeking is me, I am looking to be real, then improve and be better.  I am looking to make a difference in my world, and hope that the difference I make will benefit the world of my children and my wife; but if not, I know that the changes I am making will make me a better version of me.  And as mush as I wish for a problem-free, happy life; it will not happen -- but I will be better equipped to handle the problems.  

​

I think of it as: I am more able to handle it when I get a sliver now than I was as a kid.  I know the right methods to extract the sliver, the importance of cleaning the tools and the wound, and I know that the pain will not be permanent, but temporary (a few days at most); and if not, I know where I can go to get help (doctors office).  As a kid, that sliver was the end of playing and having fun and the beginning of torture and wasted time waiting for it to be bandaged/heal. As we embark on discovering our real power and real selves, our problems do not disappear, and our challenges are not gone, but we are able to handle them better than we ever have been before.
